text: When Lamine Yamal gets the ball on the right wing, most people watch him. Try something different. Watch everyone else.
Two defenders move towards him straight away. A third shifts across to cover.
And on the far side of the pitch, a space opens up that wasn't there a second ago.
That's the strange thing. Lamine changes the game even when he doesn't touch the ball again.
In football analysis, there's a word for this effect: gravity. Some players pull defenders towards them, like a planet pulling in everything around it.
In this video, we'll look at what that gravity does to a defence, who benefits from it, and how opponents are now trying to fight back.
A quick reminder of how fast this has happened.
Lamine made his first-team debut for Barça at fifteen.
At sixteen, he won the European Championship with Spain and became the youngest goalscorer in the tournament's history.
By eighteen, he had won the Kopa Trophy twice and finished second in the Ballon d'Or. Most players at that age are still in a youth team.
Part one. The double team.
Most coaches start with a simple plan: put your best one-against-one defender on him.
The problem is, Lamine wins enough of those duels to make that plan very risky. He can go outside, he can cut inside onto his left foot, and he can pass from either position.
So most teams quickly move to plan B. Two defenders.
Now there's a defender in front of him and a midfielder closing from inside.
But football is eleven against eleven. If two opponents are busy with one player, somebody else is free. Very often, it's the right-back overlapping outside him.
Or it's the midfielder arriving inside, into the space the second defender just left.
And Lamine is very good at choosing the moment to give it away. A defence that doubles up on him is a defence that has made a choice — and he can punish it.
That's the dilemma for every coach who faces Barça. Leave him one against one, and he might beat his man. Send two, and you leave a gap somewhere else.
There's no free option. Only the choice of which problem you'd rather have.
Part two. The far side.
Watch what happens to the whole defence when it shifts towards Lamine. The far side gets thinner.
That's where the left winger is waiting. One diagonal pass — and Lamine can play it with his left foot from the right wing — and the ball is in the space the defence abandoned.
The far-side full-back now has to defend a winger alone, often while running backwards.
A lot of the goals and chances that come from Barça's left side actually start with gravity on the right.
It's why judging a player only by goals and assists can miss so much. Sometimes his most important contribution is a pass that leads to a pass — or a run that pulls three opponents out of position.
None of that shows up in the statistics. All of it shows up in the result.
Part three. The inside run.
There's a third pattern, and it's maybe the most dangerous. When Lamine cuts inside, a midfielder often runs past him — into the channel between the full-back and the centre-back.
Now the centre-back has a problem. If he steps out to help with Lamine, the runner is free behind him. If he stays, Lamine has room to shoot.
Lamine just has to make the right choice, at the right time. A little pass into the run — and the runner is through on goal.
Players like Pedri and Fermín López have become very good at reading exactly when that run is on.
Part four. The counter-plan.
So what are opponents doing about it? The smartest teams try to stop him before he gets the ball — by pressing the player who would pass to him.
When he does receive, they try to force him outside, towards the touchline, and away from his left foot.
Some sit very deep on that side, so there's no space behind to attack.
And some do the opposite: they attack down his side of the pitch, so that he has to spend energy defending instead of attacking.

Each of those plans can work for a while. But each one costs something. Pressing high leaves space behind. Defending deep gives Barça the ball. Attacking his side means the opponent leaves gaps when they lose it.
That's the real meaning of gravity. It's not just that one player is hard to stop. It's that stopping him forces the other team to change its whole shape.
Part five. What it means.
The best players in history all had some version of this. Messi had it. Cruyff had it. Opponents built their whole plans around them, and their teammates enjoyed the space that left.
Lamine is still a teenager, and his game is still developing. He'll get stronger, his decisions will get faster, and defences will keep looking for new answers.
So next time you watch Barça, try it. When he gets the ball, take your eyes off him for a second. Watch the other ten players. That's where you'll see what he's really doing.
One question. Who had the most gravity you've ever seen — Lamine, prime Messi, or prime Neymar? Tell me in the comments.
And if you want to learn the dribbling habits that create all this, watch Play Like Lamine Yamal next.
